title: Why Picking Your Battles Is Bad Advice
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pushes back against the common advice to 'pick your battles,' which he characterizes as a lowering of standards that amounts to inconsistency—unfair to students and a driver of increasing misbehavior. He argues that it is precisely the small, seemingly inconsequential details, like how students hang up backpacks or gather into groups, that protect against big disruptions, invoking the broken windows theory as the underlying mechanism. When a lesson turns talkative or a routine gets sloppy, he contends this is not evidence that expectations should be lowered but a signal that teachers should ask for more, not less, through re-teaching and greater explicitness. He clarifies the strategy isn't fighting every battle but rather following through consistently on stated expectations so that no true 'battle' ever needs to be fought. The piece frames insistence on small details as the path to genuine, lasting peace in the classroom.
points: 'Picking your battles' is characterized as a lowering of standards that produces inconsistency and, ultimately, more misbehavior.
Small, seemingly minor details—like how backpacks are hung or groups are formed—are framed as the actual protection against major disruptions, via the broken windows theory.
A talkative lesson or sloppy routine is reframed as a signal to ask for more from students, not evidence they can't do better.
The recommended approach isn't fighting every battle, but consistently following through on stated expectations so no true battle ever arises.
Insistence on small procedural details is presented as the secret to impeccable behavior and lasting classroom peace.
quotes: When it comes to classroom management, you’ve got to pick your battles. So the advice goes.
This is a big mistake. Picking your battles is terrible advice. It amounts to a bottoming of standards, a surrendering of your beliefs and values, and a giving in and giving up on students.
You see, it’s the small, seemingly inconsequential details that protect you from the big things—the major disruptions, the dramatic incidents, the endless stress.
A talkative lesson or a lazy routine isn’t a sign that your students can’t do any better.

Taking a stand on the little things is the secret to impeccable behavior. It’s in holding students accountable for how they enter your classroom or take out their laptops or work independently that keeps disrespect and unruliness from ever entering the picture.
This doesn’t mean that you have to fight every battle. It means that you don’t fight any battle at all. Instead, you simply follow through on your promises .
